newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt hawks itself at Middle East conference.
newsitem.headline: Egypt hawks itself at Middle East conference.

text.p: Egypt is eagerly selling itself at a Middle East economic conference this week by offering investors a plethora of projects and business opportunities it hopes will rake in billions of dollars.

More than 2,000 businessmen will take part in the third Middle East and North African Economic Conference, which opens in Cairo on Tuesday. Egypt's government and business community will present them with a long list of investment proposals.

Egypt almost scrapped the conference -- aimed initially at integrating Israel into the region's economy -- after the May election of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose policies have slowed the region's peace process.
But President Hosni Mubarak decided that the conference would be a perfect showcase for his country's increasingly market-led economy and its International Monetary Fund-backed overhaul programme.

In a glossy booklet aimed at the conference delegates, Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri, who heads Egypt's economically-oriented cabinet appointed in January, trumpeted his country's achievements. He also said foreign investment would help.

"The transfer of technology through foreign investments, and the active promotion of Egyptian exports to the rest of the world, are the two most important instruments of the government's reform policy," Ganzouri said.
"Investors from all countries have the opportunity to share in Egypt's prosperity, they are welcome to participate in its reform and they are promised to reap its rewards."
The government forecasts real economic growth for the 1996/97 financial year, which began in July, at 5.0 percent compared to 4.9 percent in the previous year.
It hopes growth will hit six to seven percent a year by the end of the decade.

The government has issued two thick volumes of private and state projects to lure foreign funds. It has highlighted investment opportunities in almost all sectors of the economy ranging from the obvious -- the tourism and oil industries -- to regional information schemes.
Egypt is also trying to attract investors to regional megaprojects like a North Africa-Middle East coastal highway and a pipeline to supply Egyptian natural gas to Israel, Jordan and perhaps Turkey.
-- A $1.5 billion petrochemical manufacturing facility which will use Egypt's ample reserves of natural gas.

-- The Nile River clean-up campaign to eradicate the Nile hyacinth flower clogging up the waterways. Its private-sector promoters hope it will be a pilot project for removing the plant invading all fresh waterways throughout the region.
-- A $117.5 million project to produce sugar from sugar beet. The state, which imports large quantities of white sugar annually, wants the project to make Egypt self-sufficient.
-- Agriculture Development of East Oweinat, a $1 billion project which aims to reclaim land for cultivation and to provide water from the Nubian Aquifer located in Egypt's south.
